candidates.name: Lance Gooden
candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 5th District since 2019
candidates.background: Lance Gooden worked in the insurance industry and served three terms in the Texas House. He was first elected to Congress in 2018. He lives with his wife, Alexa, and their two children.

priorities.text: Supports free-market health care solutions to reduce costs and increase patient choice.
Opposes using taxpayer dollars to fund abortion.
Introduced the End Sanctuary Cities Act to penalize officials who interfere with federal immigration enforcement.

record.text: On the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending: voted yes on roll call 145; voted yes on roll call 190.
Voted for the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted for the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted for the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted for the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted against H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted against H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted for the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Voted for the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act (H.R. 21) in January 2025.
Voted against H.R. 8, a 2021 bill to expand background checks on gun sales, citing Second Amendment concerns.
Introduced legislation to bar the federal government from requiring elementary schools to teach gender identity and sex education.
Voted against certifying Arizona and Pennsylvania electoral votes on January 6, 2021.

q_federal_spending.summary: Voted for the 2025 reconciliation law, which reduced projected federal Medicaid spending.

q_voting_access.summary: Voted for the SAVE Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted for a bill to make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime and for a ban on Medicaid funding for such procedures for minors.

q_tariffs.summary: Voted against ending the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

q_gun_laws.summary: Voted against expanding background checks in 2021, citing the rights of law-abiding gun owners.

q_abortion.summary: Opposes taxpayer funding of abortion and voted for the Born-Alive bill.

candidates.name: Colin Allred
candidates.current_role: Attorney and former U.S. Representative
candidates.background: Colin Allred is from Dallas. He played football at Baylor University and was an NFL linebacker for five seasons before earning a law degree from the University of California, Berkeley, and working as a civil rights attorney. He served in the Obama administration at the Department of Housing and Urban Development and represented a Dallas congressional district for three terms, from 2019 to 2025. priorities.text: Campaigns on lowering costs and stopping what he calls corrupt politicians from rigging the economy.

Calls for comprehensive immigration reform with legal pathways.

record.text: Secured more than $135 million in federal funds for transportation, health care, housing and law enforcement in his former district, according to his campaign.

q_legal_status.summary: Calls for a pathway to citizenship for Dreamers and TPS holders and legal status for undocumented immigrants with continuous residency and clean records.

q_deportation.summary: Calls for abolishing ICE and ending what he describes as mass enforcement against people with no criminal record.

issue_notes.summary: Supports the End For-Profit Private Prisons Act to phase out federal immigration detention contracts.

candidates.name: Toni Rose
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 110, since 2013
candidates.background: Rose represents District 110, which includes Oak Cliff, Pleasant Grove and Balch Springs in Dallas County. She is an alumna of Paul Quinn College and previously served on City of Dallas boards, including the Planning and Zoning Commission. In the 89th Legislature she was vice chair of the House Calendars Committee and served on Appropriations and Human Services, according to her official biography.

priorities.text: Says her legislative focus is mental health, access to affordable health care and criminal justice reform.
Highlights state budget funding she secured for mental health authorities, early childhood intervention and school meal programs.

record.text: Authored HB 12, which extended postpartum Medicaid coverage for new mothers from two to 12 months, according to her official biography.

In 2025 authored HB 2402 (Medicaid fees and rates), HB 2809 (DFPS reporting on youth suicide attempts), HB 5155 (maternal opioid misuse model under Medicaid) and HB 5394, which became law, and HB 2777 to bar the death penalty for people with severe mental illness, which failed in committee.
Voted against SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on third reading.
In 2023 voted for the April 2023 budget amendment barring state funds for vouchers and for the November 2023 amendment removing education savings accounts from HB 1.
Voted for HB 2 (2025 school finance) on third reading and voted to concur in the final Senate version.
Voted for a 2025 budget amendment (Amendment No. 22 to SB 1) directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid, which failed 63 to 85.
Voted against SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (the 2025 bail constitutional amendment) and voted against SB 9 (2025 bail procedures).
Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most hemp-derived THC products, on third reading.
In 2025 voted against SB 8 (requiring certain sheriffs to enter agreements with ICE) and SB 1362 (barring enforcement of extreme risk protective orders).
In the August 2025 second special session voted against HB 4 (2025 mid-decade congressional redistricting) and against HB 7 (2025, civil lawsuits over abortion-inducing drugs).

In 2023 voted against SB 14 (ban on gender transition treatments for minors), HB 2127 (state preemption of local regulations), SB 3 (state border barrier funding) and SB 4 (state illegal entry offense).
Voted for impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton in May 2023.
Voted for Dustin Burrows over David Cook in the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker of the House.
Was recorded absent on August 5, 2025, when the House lacked a quorum during the House Democrats' walkout over congressional redistricting.

notes.text: Ran unopposed in the 2026 Democratic primary; no other candidate is listed for this seat in this guide's roster.
Named among Texas Monthly's Best Legislators in 2023, according to her official biography.

candidates.name: John Bryant
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 114, since 2023
candidates.background: Bryant served in the Texas House from 1974 to 1983 and was elected to the U.S. House in 1983, and he ran for the U.S. Senate in 1996, according to ATPE. He returned to the Texas House after winning District 114 in 2022. His campaign says Texas Monthly named him one of its Ten Best Legislators three times.

priorities.text: Says he is running because the threat to democracy requires everyone to get off the sidelines.

record.text: In 2025 authored HB 1355 (Medicaid expansion), HB 2570 (extreme risk protective orders), HB 3247 (electronic voter registration), HB 5163 and HB 5598 (minimum wage and living wage study) and HB 5156 (TRS cost-of-living adjustments); none became law.
Voted against SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on third reading.
In 2023 voted for the April 2023 budget amendment barring state funds for vouchers and for the November 2023 amendment removing education savings accounts from HB 1.
Voted for HB 2 (2025 school finance) on third reading and voted to concur in the final Senate version.
Voted for a 2025 budget amendment (Amendment No. 22 to SB 1) directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid, which failed 63 to 85.
Voted against SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (the 2025 bail constitutional amendment) and voted against SB 9 (2025 bail procedures).
Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most hemp-derived THC products, on third reading.

In 2025 voted against SB 17 (land purchases tied to designated foreign adversaries), SB 8 (requiring certain sheriffs to enter agreements with ICE) and SB 1362 (barring enforcement of extreme risk protective orders).
In the August 2025 second special session voted against HB 4 (2025 mid-decade congressional redistricting) and against HB 7 (2025, civil lawsuits over abortion-inducing drugs).

In 2023 voted against SB 14 (ban on gender transition treatments for minors), HB 2127 (state preemption of local regulations), SB 3 (state border barrier funding) and SB 4 (state illegal entry offense).
Voted for impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton in May 2023.
Was recorded absent on August 5, 2025, when the House lacked a quorum during the House Democrats' walkout over congressional redistricting.

notes.text: Was recorded present but not voting in the January 2025 Speaker runoff.
Endorsed by Texas Parent PAC in 2022, according to ATPE.

candidates.name: Brian Harrison
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 10
candidates.background: Brian Harrison represents House District 10, which covers all of Ellis County. During the Trump administration he served as chief of staff at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. He is a graduate of Ovilla Christian School.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted against HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted against the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted against the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.

Voted against HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs; a statement of vote in the journal says the member intended to vote yes.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for David Cook over Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker.
In April 2023 voted yes on the motion to table, and no on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted against Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted against HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Voted against SB 31 (2025), which clarified medical exceptions to the state abortion ban; it passed 134 to 4. In floor remarks he said it was irresponsible to change the state's pro-life protections.
Authored HB 698 and HJR 64 (2025) to abolish property taxes; neither advanced past committee.
Authored HB 847 (2025), prohibiting public funding for gender reassignment, and HB 2691 (2025), barring lobbyist expenditures and gifts to public servants; neither became law.

candidates.name: Nathaniel Moran
candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 1st District since 2023
candidates.background: Nathaniel Moran attended the U.S. Military Academy at West Point before completing degrees in Russian, an MBA and a law degree at Texas Tech University. He practiced law in Tyler, served on the Tyler City Council and was Smith County judge for six years. He was elected to Congress in 2022 and serves on the Ways and Means Committee and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.

priorities.text: Supports skills-based education that connects students with local jobs.
Supports making loans more accessible for farmers and rural communities.
Supports barring federal contracts with companies tied to forced labor in China's Xinjiang region.

record.text: On the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending: voted yes on roll call 145; voted yes on roll call 190.
Voted for the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted for the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted for the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted for the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted against H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted against H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted for the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Voted for the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act (H.R. 21) in January 2025.
Introduced the No Tax on Overtime Act to let workers deduct qualified overtime pay from taxable income.
Reintroduced the Building Youth Workforce Skills Act to expand workforce training for students.

q_federal_spending.summary: Voted for the 2025 reconciliation law, which reduced projected federal Medicaid spending.

q_voting_access.summary: Voted for the SAVE Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted for a bill to make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime and for a ban on Medicaid funding for such procedures for minors.

q_tariffs.summary: Voted against ending the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

candidates.name: Jay Dean
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 7, since 2017
candidates.background: Jay Dean of Longview has represented House District 7 since 2017. He served a decade as mayor of Longview and five years on the city council. He is general manager of Thomas Oilfield Services and a graduate of Louisiana State University.

priorities.text: Describes himself as an advocate for smaller government, responsible budgeting, low tax rates and a business-friendly environment.
Lists strengthening public education and workforce training, the right to life and the Second Amendment among his priorities.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.
In April 2023 voted no on the motion to table, and yes on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted for Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Authored HB 138 (2025), creating the Health Impact, Cost, and Coverage Analysis Program, which became law.
Authored HB 3619 (2025), on surface owner rights when the Railroad Commission plugs wells, and HB 2686 (2025), requiring registration of frac tanks; both became law.

notes.text: In the 2024 ATPE survey he said he would support vouchers "only if someone can show me how we find it in perpetuity" and without cuts to public schools; he voted for SB 2 in 2025.
In the 2024 ATPE survey he said "if we want the best schools we need to fully fund them" and supported a state-funded raise for educators.

record.text: Authored HB 1657 (2025) to create an education savings account program and HJR 84 (2025) to let the Legislature set minimum bonds for certain violent felonies; neither passed.

In 2023 voted against the April 2023 budget amendment barring state funds for vouchers and against the November 2023 amendment removing education savings accounts from HB 1.

Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (the 2025 bail constitutional amendment) and voted for SB 9 (2025 bail procedures).
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most hemp-derived THC products, on third reading.

In 2025 voted for SB 17 (land purchases tied to designated foreign adversaries), SB 8 (requiring certain sheriffs to enter agreements with ICE) and SB 1362 (barring enforcement of extreme risk protective orders).
In the August 2025 second special session voted for HB 4 (2025 mid-decade congressional redistricting) and for HB 7 (2025, civil lawsuits over abortion-inducing drugs).

candidates.name: Tom Oliverson
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 130, since 2017
candidates.background: Oliverson is a board-certified anesthesiologist and partner at US Anesthesia Partners. He represents Tomball, Cypress, Waller and Hockley. In the 89th Legislature he served on Appropriations, Redistricting and Environmental Regulation and was chair of the House Republican Caucus. He is a past president of the National Council of Insurance Legislators.

priorities.text: Describes himself as a voice for prosperity, limited government and innovative policy solutions.

record.text: In 2025 authored HB 1489 (barring officials from distributing certain voter registration forms), HB 3817 (offense of gender identity fraud) and HB 4273 (Medicaid eligibility verification), which did not become law, and HB 2038 (licensing of certain physicians) and HB 2655 (regional health programs for small employers), which did.
His HB 2243 (2025) creating a commission on teacher retention was vetoed by the governor.
Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on third reading.
In 2023 voted against the April 2023 budget amendment barring state funds for vouchers and against the November 2023 amendment removing education savings accounts from HB 1.
Voted for HB 2 (2025 school finance) on third reading and voted to concur in the final Senate version.
Voted against a 2025 budget amendment (Amendment No. 22 to SB 1) directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid, which failed 63 to 85.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (the 2025 bail constitutional amendment) and voted for SB 9 (2025 bail procedures).
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most hemp-derived THC products, on third reading.

In 2025 voted for SB 17 (land purchases tied to designated foreign adversaries), SB 8 (requiring certain sheriffs to enter agreements with ICE) and SB 1362 (barring enforcement of extreme risk protective orders).
In the August 2025 second special session voted for HB 4 (2025 mid-decade congressional redistricting) and for HB 7 (2025, civil lawsuits over abortion-inducing drugs).
In 2023 voted for SB 14 (ban on gender transition treatments for minors), HB 2127 (state preemption of local regulations), SB 3 (state border barrier funding) and SB 4 (state illegal entry offense).
Was recorded absent (excused) for the May 2023 House vote impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Voted for David Cook over Dustin Burrows in the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker of the House.

notes.text: Ran unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary and did not respond to the Community Impact or ATPE 2026 questionnaires.
Endorsed by the Texas Home School Coalition in 2016 through 2022, according to ATPE.

candidates.name: Valoree Swanson
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 150, since 2017
candidates.background: Swanson is a sixth-generation Texan who worked in commercial real estate after earning a business degree from Baylor University. She served as a State Republican Executive Committeewoman from 2006 to 2014 and as a precinct chair for more than two decades. She founded The BlueSheet, which issues Republican primary recommendations.

priorities.text: Says she wants to cut red tape and taxes and has worked to eliminate the business margins tax.
Campaigns on border security and support for the military.

record.text: In 2025 authored HB 439 (voter registration maintenance and review of mail ballots, creating offenses), HB 496 (a ballot option to vote for no candidate) and HB 1617 (exempting firearms made in Texas from federal regulation), which did not pass, and HB 551 on TEC report addresses, which became law.
Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on third reading.
In 2023 voted against the April 2023 budget amendment barring state funds for vouchers and against the November 2023 amendment removing education savings accounts from HB 1.
Voted for HB 2 (2025 school finance) on third reading and voted to concur in the final Senate version.
Voted against a 2025 budget amendment (Amendment No. 22 to SB 1) directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid, which failed 63 to 85.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (the 2025 bail constitutional amendment) and voted for SB 9 (2025 bail procedures).
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most hemp-derived THC products, on third reading.

In 2025 voted for SB 17 (land purchases tied to designated foreign adversaries), SB 8 (requiring certain sheriffs to enter agreements with ICE) and SB 1362 (barring enforcement of extreme risk protective orders).
In the August 2025 second special session voted for HB 4 (2025 mid-decade congressional redistricting) and for HB 7 (2025, civil lawsuits over abortion-inducing drugs).
In 2023 voted for SB 14 (ban on gender transition treatments for minors), HB 2127 (state preemption of local regulations), SB 3 (state border barrier funding) and SB 4 (state illegal entry offense).
Voted against impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton in May 2023.
Voted for David Cook over Dustin Burrows in the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker of the House.

notes.text: Ran unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary, according to ATPE.
Endorsed by Gov. Greg Abbott in the 2024 primary and by the Texas Home School Coalition from 2016 through 2022, according to ATPE.
Voted against adopting the conference committee report on SB 1, the 2026 to 2027 state budget, in 2025.

candidates.name: Monica De La Cruz
candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 15th District since 2023
candidates.background: Monica De La Cruz is a former insurance agent who owned an insurance agency in the Rio Grande Valley. She was elected in 2022 as the first Latina and first Republican to represent the 15th District. She created the South Texas Water Working Group.

priorities.text: Calls for completing border infrastructure and reinstating the Remain in Mexico policy.
Supports oil and natural gas jobs, cutting regulations that raise energy costs and the safe use of nuclear energy.
Pledges to protect Medicare and Social Security.
Presses Mexico to meet its water treaty obligations to South Texas farmers.

record.text: On the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending: voted yes on roll call 145; voted yes on roll call 190.
Voted for the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Did not vote on the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted for the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted for the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted against H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted for H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted for the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.

candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 25th District since 2013
candidates.background: Roger Williams was raised in Fort Worth, attended Texas Christian University and played in the Atlanta Braves farm system. He runs a family-owned car dealership and cattle operation and coached baseball at TCU. He was first elected to Congress in 2012 and lives in Weatherford.

priorities.text: Prioritizes lower taxes and federal spending cuts.
Prioritizes deregulation and help for small businesses.
Prioritizes border security and support for Israel.

record.text: On the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending: voted yes on roll call 145; voted yes on roll call 190.
Did not vote on the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted for the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted for the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted for the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted against H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted against H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted for the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Did not vote on the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act (H.R. 21) in January 2025.
Introduced the Bulletproof Law Enforcement Vehicles Act to allow federal funds for police vehicle security upgrades.

q_federal_spending.summary: Voted for the 2025 reconciliation law, which reduced projected federal Medicaid spending.

q_voting_access.summary: Voted for the SAVE Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

q_tariffs.summary: Voted against ending the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

candidates.name: Keith Bell
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 4, since 2019
candidates.background: Keith Bell of Forney has represented House District 4 since 2019. He founded Intex Electrical Contractors in 1983, holds a master electrician license and served 20 years on the Forney ISD school board. He is a graduate of Dallas Baptist University.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Was absent for the vote on SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.
In April 2023 voted yes on the motion to table, and yes on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted for Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Authored HB 12 (2025), on review and audit of state agency operations, and HB 120 (2025), on college, career and military readiness and career and technology education; both became law.
Authored HB 5033 (2025), relating to the state authority to run a vehicle emissions inspection program, which became law.
Filed HB 264 (2025) to dedicate certain surplus state revenue to property tax relief and HJR 36 to allow a lower homestead appraisal cap; neither passed.

notes.text: In a 2018 ATPE survey he answered "No!" when asked whether he would vote for any voucher or education savings account program; he voted for SB 2 in 2025.
Endorsed by Texas Parent PAC in the 2018 and 2022 general elections, according to ATPE.

candidates.name: Angelia Orr
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 13, since 2023
candidates.background: Angelia Orr of Hill County has represented House District 13 since 2023. She is a small business owner, former substitute teacher and former Itasca ISD trustee, and she served as Hill County district clerk. She graduated from Texas A&M University in 1992.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.

Was absent for the vote on the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill; a statement of vote in the journal says the member would have voted yes.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.
In April 2023 voted yes on the motion to table, and yes on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted against Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Authored HB 24 (2025), on procedures for zoning changes, and HB 128 (2025), on sister-city agreements with foreign countries; both became law.
Authored HB 3801 (2025), creating the Health Professions Workforce Coordinating Council, which became law.

notes.text: In a 2022 ATPE survey she wrote that she was against any type of voucher program; she later voted for voucher legislation in 2023 and 2025.
The Waco Tribune-Herald editorial board urged voters to oppose her in the 2024 primary, citing the change in her voucher position, and Gov. Greg Abbott endorsed her, according to ATPE.

q_vouchers.summary: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program.

q_school_funding.summary: Voted for HB 2 (2025), the school finance and teacher pay bill, on House passage and final concurrence.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in classrooms.

q_medicaid.summary: Voted against a 2025 budget amendment directing the state to seek a waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility.

q_bail.summary: Voted for SJR 5 and SB 9 (2025), which expand denial of bail and tighten bail procedures for violent felony charges.

q_cannabis.summary: Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products.

q_foreign_land.summary: Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to foreign adversary nations.

q_deportation.summary: Voted for SB 8 (2025), requiring certain sheriffs to seek immigration enforcement agreements with ICE.

q_gun_laws.summary: Voted for SB 1362 (2025), which bars recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective (red flag) orders.

q_abortion.summary: Voted for HB 7 (2025), allowing civil suits over the distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted for SB 14 (2023), which prohibits gender transition medical treatments for minors.

q_preemption.summary: Voted for final passage of HB 2127 (2023), which limits local regulations in fields occupied by state law.

q_border_state.summary: Voted for SB 3 (2023, fourth called session), funding state border barrier construction and border operations.

candidates.background: Will Metcalf is a sixth-generation Montgomery County resident who has represented House District 16 since 2015. priorities.text: Calls property tax relief and long-term predictability for homeowners and businesses crucial priorities.

promises.text: Says he would lower appraisal caps, raise the state share of school funding and fully eliminate school maintenance and operations property taxes.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.

candidates.name: Craig Goldman
candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 12th District since 2025
candidates.background: Craig Goldman is a Fort Worth native with a degree from the University of Texas at Austin. He worked at his family's gourmet food and wine store. He served 12 years in the Texas House, where he chaired the Energy Resources Committee, before his election to Congress in 2024.

priorities.text: Prioritizes border security and the American taxpayer.
Prioritizes reducing taxes and strengthening national defense.
Pledges to fiercely protect Second Amendment rights.

record.text: On the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending: voted yes on roll call 145; voted yes on roll call 190.
Voted for the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted for the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted for the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted for the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted against H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted against H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted for the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Voted for the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act (H.R. 21) in January 2025.
As a state representative, authored House Bill 6 in 2023, creating a criminal offense for fentanyl-related deaths, according to his campaign.
Introduced the Better Care, Better Cost Act on Medicaid managed care incentives and the Abraham Accords Expansion Act of 2026.
Says he passed what he calls the strongest election integrity bill in Texas history as a state representative.

q_federal_spending.summary: Voted for the 2025 reconciliation law, which reduced projected federal Medicaid spending.

q_voting_access.summary: Passed a Texas election bill targeting ballot harvesting and voted for the SAVE Act.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted in the Texas House to ban gender transition surgeries on minors and voted for federal bills restricting such treatments.

q_tariffs.summary: Voted against ending the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

q_border_state.summary: Says he voted in the Texas House for record border security funding and the use of the National Guard.

q_abortion.summary: Supported the Texas Heartbeat bill and voted to defund abortion providers as a state representative.

q_gun_laws.summary: Says he will fiercely protect Second Amendment rights and is endorsed by the NRA.

candidates.name: Cole Hefner
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 5, since 2017
candidates.background: Cole Hefner of Mount Pleasant has represented House District 5 since 2017. He previously served as an Upshur County commissioner, owned a construction business for 16 years and now owns an insurance business. In 2025 he chaired the House Homeland Security, Public Safety and Veterans' Affairs Committee.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.
In April 2023 voted yes on the motion to table, and no on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted against Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Authored HB 17 (2025) to restrict purchases of Texas real property by certain foreign individuals and entities; it was left pending in committee.
Authored HB 4675 (2025), creating an offense for firearm possession by a person not lawfully present in the United States; it was reported from committee but did not become law.
Authored HB 2464 (2025), on municipal regulation of home-based businesses, and HB 4264 (2025), a grant program for peace officers with master proficiency certificates; both became law.

candidates.name: Lauren B. Peña
candidates.current_role: Founder and CEO of Peña Legal Advocacy
candidates.background: Lauren B. Peña is originally from Harrisonburg, Virginia, and holds a political science degree from Southern New Hampshire University. She founded Peña Legal Advocacy, a faith-based nonprofit legal and policy group, and serves on the Austin Community Police Review Commission. She lives in Austin with her partner and six children. This is her first run for public office.

priorities.text: Plans to reduce taxes, increase take-home pay and enforce a balanced budget.
Says she will expand vocational training and ensure welfare is a bridge to work.
Says she will defend parental rights and protect children from exploitation.

promises.text: Plans to introduce the Sex Offender Deterrence Act to end automatic protective custody for convicted sex offenders.

q_federal_spending.summary: Supports a balanced budget and says welfare should be a bridge to work.

issue_notes.summary: Says she will unleash American energy and calls energy independence a national security and cost of living issue.
Opposes government mandates on personal medical decisions.

candidates.name: Greg Casar
candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 35th District since 2023
candidates.background: Greg Casar is a native Texan and son of Mexican immigrants who graduated from the University of Virginia. He worked as a labor organizer and policy director at the Workers Defense Project and served on the Austin City Council from 2015 to 2022. He was elected to Congress in 2022 and is running in the redrawn 37th District. He lives in Austin with his spouse, Asha.

priorities.text: Campaigns on good jobs, reproductive rights, Medicare for All and ending the climate crisis.
Supports federal legislation to end partisan gerrymandering and restore the Voting Rights Act.
Supports ending the filibuster and expanding the U.S. Supreme Court.
Does not accept corporate PAC donations and supports overturning Citizens United.

record.text: On the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending: voted no on roll call 145; voted no on roll call 190.
Voted against the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted against the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted against the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Did not vote on the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted for H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted for H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted against the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Voted against the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 7148) in January 2026.
Introduced the Double the Wage for Overtime Act.
As an Austin City Council member, ended arrests and citations for personal marijuana use in Austin, according to his campaign.
Co-leads the New Way Forward Act and cosponsors the Women's Health Protection Act and the Assault Weapons Ban.

q_federal_spending.summary: Voted against the 2025 reconciliation law, which reduced projected federal Medicaid spending.

q_voting_access.summary: Cosponsors the Freedom to Vote Act, which would establish automatic voter registration.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted against a bill to make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime.

q_tariffs.summary: Voted for a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

q_cannabis.summary: Supports legalizing marijuana and expunging past records.

q_abortion.summary: Supports making Roe v. Wade federal law and cosponsors the Women's Health Protection Act.

q_gun_laws.summary: Supports universal background checks, ending permitless carry and banning assault weapons.

q_legal_status.summary: Supports the American Dream and Promise Act and related bills offering legal status to immigrants.

q_deportation.summary: Says immigrant families deserve to live free from fear of separation and deportation.

q_border_state.summary: Co-leads a bill he says would roll back Gov. Abbott's militarization of the border.

q_medicaid.summary: Cosponsors Medicare for All, which goes beyond Medicaid expansion.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Supports the Green New Deal and union jobs in clean energy.

q_min_wage.summary: Led efforts on the Austin City Council to raise the minimum wage, according to his campaign.

candidates.name: Aj Louderback
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 30, since 2025
candidates.background: AJ Louderback was elected to House District 30 in 2024 and serves in the 89th Legislature.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for David Cook over Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker.
Authored HB 2257 (2025), requiring county sheriffs to enter agreements with the federal government to enforce immigration law; it did not pass, and the House later passed the similar SB 8.
Authored HB 3778 (2025), on using geothermal energy as a dispatchable generation resource, and HB 1487 (2025), removing the fee for a license to carry a handgun; neither became law.
Authored HB 2820 (2025), on charitable bingo operating capital, which became law.

candidates.name: Crystal Sedillo
candidates.current_role: Democratic nominee for Texas House District 30
candidates.background: Crystal Sedillo was born in Wharton County and raised in Matagorda County. She holds a communication degree from Texas A&M University-Victoria and spent four years working in education.

priorities.text: Says health care should be a right, not a luxury, and supports expanding Medicaid.
Wants every child to have access to a quality public education regardless of ZIP code or income.
Calls for a moratorium on new data centers until safeguards protect water, the grid, landowners and communities.
Lists lowering the cost of living, raising the minimum wage and investing in infrastructure.

notes.text: Had not responded to the 2026 ATPE candidate survey.

q_medicaid.summary: Supports expanding Medicaid, which she says would cover more than 600,000 Texans.

q_vouchers.summary: Opposes school vouchers, saying they compete for dollars public schools need.

q_school_funding.summary: Supports fully funding public schools and supporting educators and staff.

q_min_wage.summary: Lists raising the minimum wage as part of her affordability agenda.

q_legal_status.summary: Supports affordable pathways to citizenship.

q_deportation.summary: Supports deporting immigrants with criminal records but opposes deporting working families without due process.

q_gun_laws.summary: Supports Second Amendment rights along with a purchase age of 21 and red flag laws.

q_water.summary: Calls for investing in water infrastructure, conservation, reuse and desalination.

candidates.background: Terry Wilson of Georgetown is a retired U.S. Army colonel with more than 30 years of service and a former Department of Defense acquisition executive. He holds a business degree from Texas A&M University and a master's degree from the Air War College system.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).

Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.

candidates.name: Theodore Schramm
candidates.current_role: Stay-at-home father; marketing and operations professional
candidates.background: Schramm describes himself as a stay-at-home father with professional experience in marketing, logistics, operations and project management. He ran unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary for District 136, which covers Round Rock, Cedar Park, Brushy Creek and Northwest Austin.

priorities.text: Campaigns on raising the state share of public school funding to at least 45 percent without raising overall taxes.
Supports expanding affordable care through sliding-scale clinics and telehealth, but not full Medicaid expansion.
Campaigns on appraisal audits, larger homestead exemptions and capping property tax and utility increases at inflation.
Campaigns on auditing I-35 projects and prioritizing managed lanes and express buses.

promises.text: Proposes requiring voter referendums for major expenditures over $50 million.

q_school_funding.summary: Wants the state share of school funding raised to at least 45 percent, paired with spending audits.

q_medicaid.summary: Supports state programs such as sliding-scale clinics but not full Medicaid expansion.

q_abortion.summary: Describes himself as pro-life from conception but would allow limited exceptions such as health risks and stillbirths.

q_gun_laws.summary: Supports the Second Amendment and sensible background checks to keep firearms from dangerous individuals.

q_cannabis.summary: Supports decriminalizing small amounts of cannabis and studying legalization.

candidates.name: John H. Bucy, III
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 136, since 2019
candidates.background: Bucy is a small business owner whose organization runs athletic, academic and arts competitions for public school students. He represents parts of Williamson County, including Northwest Austin, Cedar Park and Round Rock. He was vice chair of the House Elections Committee in the 89th Legislature and holds a degree from Austin College.

priorities.text: Campaigns on strong public schools, access to health care, good jobs, equality and the freedom to vote.

record.text: Offered the 2025 budget amendment directing HHSC to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid, which failed 63 to 85.

In 2025 authored HB 197, HB 262 and HJR 21 (Medicaid expansion), HB 417 and HB 1917 (mail voting for any qualified voter), HB 311 (electronic voter registration), HB 454 (abolishing the death penalty) and HB 2975 (regulating cannabis); none became law.
Voted against SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on third reading.
In 2023 voted for the April 2023 budget amendment barring state funds for vouchers and for the November 2023 amendment removing education savings accounts from HB 1.
Voted for HB 2 (2025 school finance) on third reading and voted to concur in the final Senate version.
Voted for a 2025 budget amendment (Amendment No. 22 to SB 1) directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid, which failed 63 to 85.
Voted against SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (the 2025 bail constitutional amendment) and voted against SB 9 (2025 bail procedures).
Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most hemp-derived THC products, on third reading.

In 2025 voted against SB 17 (land purchases tied to designated foreign adversaries), SB 8 (requiring certain sheriffs to enter agreements with ICE) and SB 1362 (barring enforcement of extreme risk protective orders).
In the August 2025 second special session voted against HB 4 (2025 mid-decade congressional redistricting) and against HB 7 (2025, civil lawsuits over abortion-inducing drugs).

In 2023 voted against SB 14 (ban on gender transition treatments for minors), HB 2127 (state preemption of local regulations), SB 3 (state border barrier funding) and SB 4 (state illegal entry offense).
Voted for impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton in May 2023.
Voted for Dustin Burrows over David Cook in the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker of the House.
Was recorded absent on August 5, 2025, when the House lacked a quorum during the House Democrats' walkout over congressional redistricting.

notes.text: Ran unopposed in the 2026 Democratic primary, according to ATPE.
Endorsed by Texas Parent PAC in 2018, 2020 and 2022, according to ATPE.

candidates.name: Ryan Guillen
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 31; chair of the House Homeland Security and Public Safety Committee
candidates.background: Ryan Guillen was elected to the Legislature at age 24. He holds an agriculture degree from Texas A&M University, worked as a high school agriculture teacher, and grew up working at his family's feed store and ranch. In 2025 he chaired the House Committee on Homeland Security and Public Safety.

priorities.text: His House biography describes him as an advocate for creating jobs, cutting taxes and red tape, and reducing over-testing.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Was absent for the vote on SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms; a statement of vote in the journal says the member would have voted yes.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted for Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for David Cook over Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker.
In April 2023 voted yes on the motion to table, and no on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted against Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Authored HB 101 (2025), creating the Texas State Guard Professionalization Task Force, and HB 2516 (2025), on Medicare supplement plans for people under 65; both became law.
Authored HJR 34 (2025), a property tax exemption constitutional amendment that was filed with the Secretary of State for voter approval, and filed border security bills including HB 176 and HB 246.

candidates.name: Jennifer "Jj" Dominguez
candidates.current_role: Licensed clinical social worker; chair of the Wilson County Democratic Party
candidates.background: Jennifer "JJ" Dominguez is a licensed clinical social worker who chairs the Wilson County Democratic Party. She moved to Texas from Illinois 20 years ago, spent 14 years as a dialysis social worker in rural Texas, and now provides therapy to immigrants. She lives in Floresville.

priorities.text: Lists investing in educators, fully funding public schools and protecting local control as top priorities.
Calls health care a fundamental human right and wants to address rural hospital and clinic closures.
Proposes free statewide mental health services and expanded rural telehealth.
Calls for better rural roads, water systems and internet access.

q_min_wage.summary: Supports raising the minimum wage to $15 an hour, indexed for inflation.

q_vouchers.summary: Supports repealing private school vouchers and told ATPE that public schools should be fully funded before expanding ESAs.

q_school_funding.summary: Told ATPE that Texas should provide additional, sustainable funding for public schools and a state-funded raise for educators.

q_medicaid.summary: Supports universal coverage and reducing barriers to Medicaid.

q_voting_access.summary: Supports countywide voting and making voting more accessible during emergencies.
